source.primary: CDC/NCHS Vital Statistics Reporting Guidance Report No. 1 (Oct 2017)

coverage_notes: Includes all 13 scenario/example certificates in the 2017 guide (1 figure example + Scenarios A, B + Appendix II Scenarios I-X) and all additional cases in the training deck (Oso, 2 state-comparison cases, 3 slide-24 examples, 2 Part II natural examples, 1 Part I certificate fragment). Deck scenarios B, C, D, I, II, III, IV duplicate guide scenarios and are cross-referenced in also_in rather than repeated.
The MDI Quick Guide has no worked cases; it contributes only cause-of-death lists (see cdc_rules.json mdi_quick_guide_cause_lists).

CDC documents contain NO worked 'not_related' or 'possible' scenario; gold contains none. Use irma_table/uri_table 'possible' rows (homicide, suicide, undetermined; Uri fire/CO/hypothermia possible) as evidence for that class.

label_confidence: 'stated' = CDC text explicitly calls it indirectly related; 'implied' = CDC says 'disaster-related' (deck answers 'Yes') or gives the certificate and the direct/indirect label follows from Box 3 / Box 4 / flowchart wording. No guide scenario carries an explicit direct/indirect stamp.
Certificates: Part I lines are in extracted order; manner-of-death checkboxes are graphics and not extractable (null).

scenarios.narrative: A 59-year-old female died 3 days after Hurricane Sandy. The storm caused a regional blackout. She was found in her house. A generator was running on the first floor of the home. According to emergency management officials, the carbon monoxide fumes inside the home were three times the danger level. She had a history of emphysema and long-term tobacco use.

certificate.how_injury_occurred: Carbon monoxide source was a generator located in the home due to power outage after Hurricane Sandy
certificate.note: Part I line order (a,b,c) follows extracted text order; Manner-of-death checkbox is a graphic in the PDF and is not recoverable from extracted text; left null.

scenarios.notes: Guide p. 4 text gives 'carbon monoxide poisoning due to use of a generator ... after a storm because of a prolonged power outage' as its example of an indirect death. This simulated certificate matches that example. Emphysema is a contributing condition.

scenarios.notes: Falling trees/flying debris are direct consequences of storm forces (flowchart: 'Flying debris, falling trees'; Box 3 blunt-force trauma). Guide comment: 'This example links the head injury to a tree limb dislodged during the hurricane.' Irma MMWR also codes tree-related injuries as direct. CDC does not stamp this scenario 'direct' or 'indirect'; label inferred from the guide's Box 3 / Box 4 / flowchart.
scenarios.guide_comment: Unless the injury is the result of a fall, consider using terms other than 'fall' to describe falling debris, to avoid confusion.

scenarios.narrative: A 39-year-old male was within 4 miles of an improvised nuclear device that was detonated in a major metropolitan area. The event was confirmed by the local emergency manager and FBI as an act of terrorism. The decedent was exposed to a radiation dose of 8 grays (800 rem) as a result of prompt radiation and radioactive fallout. He also had minor traumatic injuries and thermal burns on 15% of his total body surface area. He self-evacuated to a hospital 50 miles away. He developed acute radiation syndrome, starting with intractable vomiting approximately 1 hour after the explosion, followed by bone marrow depletion of granulocyte progenitors on day 2 of hospitalization. He survived for 23 days before expiring from gram-negative sepsis, despite receiving granulocyte colony-stimulating factors, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and multiple transfusions.

certificate.part2: Thermal burns, cutaneous radiation injury, cutaneous lacerations
certificate.how_injury_occurred: Intentional detonation of nuclear device by another person as an act of terrorism
certificate.note: Part I line order (a,b,c) follows extracted text order; Manner-of-death checkbox is a graphic in the PDF and is not recoverable from extracted text; left null.

scenarios.notes: Radiation effects are a Step 2a (direct) prompt; direct definition names 'radiation ... exposure'. Guide comment: 'Delayed deaths may occur from initial blast injuries and acute radiation syndrome.' Death 23 days later by sepsis is still the direct consequence. CDC does not stamp this scenario 'direct' or 'indirect'; label inferred from the guide's Box 3 / Box 4 / flowchart.

Toxicological and alcohol screenings were negative.

scenarios.disaster_type: heat wave / derecho (East Coast derecho and heat wave)
scenarios.narrative: An 85-year-old male with a known history of arteriosclerosis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease was reported unconscious in his home. The temperature in the home was 86 degrees Fahrenheit during the East Coast derecho and heat wave, as reported by local NWS and weather stations in a major metropolitan area. He died 2 days later in the intensive care unit with a discharge diagnosis of multi-organ failure from complications of heat stroke. EMS reported that he lived alone and had a functioning air conditioner that was not on; his family indicated that he was concerned about his electric bill.

certificate.part2: Arteriosclerosis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
certificate.how_injury_occurred: Functioning air conditioner in home but not on during the East Coast derecho and heat wave
certificate.note: Part I line order (a,b,c) follows extracted text order; Manner-of-death checkbox is a graphic in the PDF and is not recoverable from extracted text; left null.

scenarios.notes: Hyperthermia is a Box 3 direct cause; the heat wave itself is the hazard and the air conditioner was functioning (no utility loss). Contrast Irma MMWR, which codes heat deaths caused by power-outage loss of A/C as indirect. Borderline case: a classifier could argue indirect because of behavioral/chronic-disease contribution.
scenarios.ambiguity: Heat from weather = direct (Box 3); heat from utility loss = indirect (Irma practice).
scenarios.guide_comment: Lack of air conditioning is a contributor for many heat-associated deaths, and medical history can be used to identify vulnerable populations for outreach.
